summaries.gardner: Lockheed Martin is the dominant incumbent in a mature, government-funded industry rather than a Rule Breaker leading an emerging one, and its CEO is a hired professional, not a founder. It has a top-tier brand in defense and real momentum from missile-defense demand, but revenue grew only about 4% a year from 2022 to 2025, so it fits Gardner's approach weakly.
summaries.buffett: Lockheed has an easy-to-grasp, durable franchise (sole-source F-35, THAAD, PAC-3 MSE, Trident II D5), converts profit to cash (FY2025 free cash flow $6,908M vs net earnings $5,017M) and has raised its dividend 24 years running. Against that, margins have slipped and $20.5B of debt with only $8.8B of equity, plus a price near 20x trailing earnings, mean it meets Buffett's quality tests better than his price tests.
summaries.munger: Munger would like the efficient-scale monopolies and 40-year sustainment tails, and the simplicity of a business whose customer is the US government. He would also note the single-customer dependence, fixed-price program losses ($1,615M of segment losses in 2025) and a full valuation, so it is a sound business at a fair-to-full price rather than a bargain.
summaries.lynch: In Lynch's terms Lockheed is a classic stalwart with a simple story: defense budgets and munitions restocking drive a record $230.4B backlog. At about 20x trailing and 18x forward earnings against EPS growth of roughly 7% after 2026's rebound, the PEG is well above 1, so the stock looks fully priced by his yardstick.
summaries.fisher: Lockheed keeps developing new products (PAC-3 ACE, Sanctum counter-drone, Golden Dome space-based interceptors, Next Generation Interceptor) and its R&D lands large production programs, which Fisher would credit. But thin, declining margins (operating margin 13.2% in 2020 to 10.3% in 2025) and repeated program charges fall short of his profitability points, so it fits partly.
summaries.graham: Lockheed is large, profitable every year and has paid rising dividends for 24 consecutive years, and EPS grew from $11.46 (2015) to $21.49 (2025). It fails Graham's valuation tests clearly: about 23x three-year average EPS and P/E times P/B near 370, because heavy buybacks have shrunk book equity to $8.8B.
summaries.thiel: Lockheed holds genuine monopolies (the only Western fifth-generation fighter in production, THAAD, Trident II D5) and excellent government distribution, which Thiel values. But its technology edge is incremental rather than ten times better in new markets, and it is the incumbent that Thiel-backed challengers like Anduril aim to disrupt.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner looks for durable growth at a reasonable price led by teams adapting to big shifts; Lockheed offers about 8% guided 2026 sales growth and a forward P/E near 18, cheaper than RTX, with rising defense demand. Its growth is not tied to a platform shift like AI and its software-era adaptation is unproven, so it is a partial fit.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller would see a clear catalyst set: raised 2026 guidance (EPS $29.95-30.65 vs $21.49 in 2025), a $35B THAAD contract, Golden Dome and Q3 results on October 22, 2026, with the stock up about 9.5% in the week to October 16. But the EPS jump is mostly a rebound from 2025 charges and next-year growth is modest, so it is not an obvious concentrated bet.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith wants high returns on capital, high gross margins and strong cash conversion; Lockheed's cash conversion and ~27% ROIC are good, but a 10.2% gross margin and leverage-inflated returns on tiny equity fall short of his quality bar. At about 20x trailing earnings it is not obviously cheap either.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula Lockheed scores well on return on capital but only middling on earnings yield, with operating profit of $7,731M against an enterprise value of about $144B (about 5.4%). It would rank as a decent but not top-decile pick.
summaries.akre: Akre's three legs are a great business, talented and honest managers, and the ability to reinvest at high returns. Lockheed has a strong moat and capable management, but it cannot reinvest most of its cash at high returns and instead pays it out in dividends and buybacks, so it fits only partly.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai's Dhandho approach seeks simple, durable businesses at deep discounts with low downside. Lockheed is simple and durable with low risk of permanent loss, but at $552 there is no deep discount: a conservative DCF at a 12% discount rate gives only about $300 per share.
summaries.wood: Lockheed is not a leader in ARK's innovation platforms (AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain, multiomics) and its costs do not fall exponentially with volume. Its counter-drone, autonomy and space work touch ARK themes only at the edges, so it does not fit Wood's disruptive-innovation approach.
summaries.ackman: Ackman likes simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with high barriers to entry, which Lockheed largely is. However, its pricing is set by a single government customer, it carries $20.5B of debt, and the valuation is full, so it is a moderate fit with no obvious activist angle.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep favoured scale-economics-shared businesses that grow ever stronger by passing savings to customers. Lockheed's scale lowers unit costs on long production runs like the F-35, but cost-plus contracts pass savings through by rule rather than strategy and its position is defended by incumbency, so it fits Sleep's model only weakly.
summaries.valentine: Valentine looked for huge, fast-growing markets and products that solve big problems for many buyers; defense is a large, rising market and Lockheed's products solve a painful security problem. But the market is controlled by a few government buyers and grows in single digits, far from the venture-style opportunity he sought.
summaries.nash: Lockheed fails most of Nash's hard filters: revenue grew 5.6% in 2025, operating margin is about 10%, debt far exceeds cash, it missed earnings estimates in two of the last four quarters, and his DCF at 12% values it near $300 versus a $552 price. It scores well on moat, ownership and the 13-category total (about 75, borderline), but overall it is a stalwart, not a Nash-style compounder.

momentum.evidence: The stock closed at $552.09 on Oct 16, 2026, about 15% higher over 12 months on a dividend-adjusted basis versus about 13% for SPY, and jumped from $504.02 on Oct 13 to $552.09 on Oct 16.

g4.evidence: CEO Jim Taiclet (ex-American Tower CEO, Air Force pilot) runs a capable team and institutions own about 76% of shares, but there is no famous visionary investor or backer beyond index and institutional holders.

g6.evidence: Analysts rate it a consensus Buy with a $618.86 average target (23 analysts, Oct 2026), and at about 18x forward earnings it is usually called fairly valued rather than overvalued.

simple.evidence: Lockheed sells fighter jets, helicopters, missiles and satellites mostly to the US government through four clear segments, a business a careful generalist can understand.

b2.evidence: It has been profitable every year with steady cash flow, but sales dipped in 2022 and net earnings fell from $6,920M (2023) to $5,017M (2025) on program losses.

integrity.evidence: Management discloses program losses clearly and returns cash via 24 straight years of dividend raises and buybacks, but the 2025 classified-program and helicopter charges ($1,615M) surprised investors and pay is tied mainly to EPS, cash flow and ROIC.

b6.evidence: Growth has been mostly organic and focused on defense, though it tried to buy Aerojet Rocketdyne (abandoned in 2022 after an FTC challenge) and agreed in 2026 to buy Ultra Maritime for $3.45B.

roic.evidence: ROIC is about 27% (StockAnalysis, TTM), but it is flattered by tiny equity ($8,768M) after buybacks and relies on $20,538M of debt.

fcf.evidence: FY2025 free cash flow was $6,908M against net earnings of $5,017M, and 2026 guidance is $7.0-7.2B.

b10.evidence: Lockheed pays out nearly all its cash ($3,000M buybacks and $3,131M dividends in 2025), and the diluted share count fell from 281.2M (2020) to 233.5M (2025), so little is retained to test this.

safety.evidence: At $552.09 the stock trades near 20x trailing EPS and a Nash-style DCF at a 12% discount rate gives about $298 per share, so there is no margin of safety.

fairprice.evidence: A forward P/E near 18 for a business with a record $230.4B backlog and a 2.6% dividend yield is reasonable, but EPS growth of about 7% after 2026 makes it full rather than cheap.

mu5.evidence: With sole-source franchises, a $230.4B backlog and the US government as main customer, the main failure paths are a sharp F-35 cut or huge fixed-price losses, both unlikely to be fatal.

reinvest.evidence: Capex is only about $1.6-2.4B a year, so most cash goes to dividends and buybacks rather than high-return reinvestment.

ly2.evidence: It is a clear stalwart: a large, steady defense prime whose story is rising defense budgets, munitions restocking and missile defense.

ly3.evidence: The trailing P/E is about 20 and forward P/E about 18, while EPS growth after 2026's rebound is expected near 7%, so P/E is well above the growth rate.

runway.evidence: Missile defense (THAAD output to quadruple), Golden Dome and European demand give years of growth, but analysts expect only about 6-7% annual revenue growth through 2028.

ly7.evidence: Diluted shares fell from 281.2M in 2020 to 231.1M in Q2 2026, but there were no buybacks in the first half of 2026 and insiders are small net sellers, not buyers.

ly8.evidence: Lockheed is widely covered (23 analysts) and about 76% institutionally owned, so it is not overlooked.

fi2.evidence: It is developing PAC-3 ACE, space-based interceptors for Golden Dome, the Next Generation Interceptor, a twice-range GMLRS successor and Sanctum counter-drone systems as older programs mature.

fi3.evidence: R&D has produced winning franchises (F-35, PAC-3 MSE, PrSM, NGI), but it lost the Air Force's sixth-generation fighter to Boeing and the Army's long-range assault aircraft to Bell.

fi4.evidence: Its government and international business development is formidable: Q2 2026 book-to-bill was 3.2 to 1 and backlog reached a record $230.4B.

longterm.evidence: Management invested ahead of demand in munitions capacity (new Courtland and Troy, Alabama facilities), but also prioritises steady dividends and buybacks.

gr1.evidence: Lockheed had $75,048M of 2025 sales and a market value of about $128B.

gr4.evidence: The October 2026 increase to $3.60 a quarter was its 24th consecutive year of dividend increases.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $11.46 in 2015 (FY2015 10-K, Selected Financial Data) to $21.49 in 2025, up about 88%.

gr6.evidence: At $552.09 the price is about 23x the 2023-2025 average diluted EPS of $23.78.

gr7.evidence: P/E of about 26 on 2025 EPS times P/B of about 14.6 gives roughly 370, far above 22.5.

timing.evidence: Wars in Ukraine and the Middle East have driven urgent restocking of interceptors, with a $35B THAAD award and Golden Dome space-based interceptor work in 2026.

th3.evidence: Lockheed is a mature giant formed in 1995 that already dominates large markets rather than a company expanding from a small niche.

team.evidence: Taiclet and CFO Evan Scott run a competent professional team that raised 2026 guidance, but it is not a founder-led or exceptional world-class team.
